slides.text: Welcome to practicals three and four. The goal is to learn to spot data types and structure in your own dataset, by asking five simple questions about every column.
The five questions are about the level of measurement, discrete versus continuous, structured versus semi-structured, text data basics, and time series behaviour.

First ask: are the values labels or numbers, and can you rank them or measure real distance? Nominal: categories with no order, like city or blood type. Ordinal: categories that can be ranked, like satisfaction or star rating. Interval: equal spacing but no true zero, like temperature in Celsius. Ratio: equal spacing with a true zero, like height, age or income.

Here is a quick test for any column. If the values are words, ask whether the categories can be ranked: no order means nominal, an order means ordinal. If the values are numbers, ask whether zero means none at all. No true zero means interval; a true zero means ratio. Zero degrees Celsius does not mean no temperature, so temperature is interval, while zero income means no income, so it is ratio.

Both are numeric. The test is whether you can count the values or must measure them. If you can list every possible value, one, two, three, with nothing in between, it is discrete: number of children, orders, clicks, defective items. If the value could fall anywhere between two numbers, it is continuous: height, temperature, time taken, weight.

Look at how the file itself is laid out, not just the values inside it. A C S V file, an Excel sheet or a database table is structured, with fixed rows and columns. A J S O N or X M L file, a log file or an email has keys or tags but no fixed table shape, and fields can differ between records.

Free-form text columns need to be broken down before you can analyse them. Raw text is a full sentence or comment as written. Tokens are the individual words or symbols. Text is organised in layers: character, word, sentence, paragraph, document. And open-ended answers differ from fixed-label text columns like yes or no. For example, the sentence I loved this product becomes the tokens I, loved, this, product, and an exclamation mark.

If your data has a date or time column, check whether values move over time in two ways. Trend is the overall direction in the long run, ignoring short wiggles. Seasonality is a pattern that repeats at fixed intervals, caused by seasons, holidays or habits. Plot values against date: a rising or falling line is a trend, regular repeating bumps are seasonality.

Your cheat sheet. Words or numbers: categorical versus numeric. Can categories be ranked: nominal versus ordinal. Does zero mean none: interval versus ratio. Can you count every value: discrete versus continuous. Rows and columns or tags and keys: structured versus semi-structured. Open-ended sentences: text data. A repeating date column: time series, trend and seasonality. Apply these questions to your own dataset. Thanks for watching.
